The word soul has several distinct meanings. All of them share a common thread — depth, inner truth, and what is most essential — but each applies in a different context. Here is a complete account of every meaning.
1. The non-physical, inner part of a person

This is the oldest and most central meaning. The soul is believed to be the part of you that is not your body — not flesh, bone, or brain. It is thought to be the seat of your consciousness, your emotions, your will, and your identity. While your body is what others can see and touch, your soul is the deeper "you" — the inner self that feels, chooses, loves, and suffers.

A key idea is that the soul can exist independently of the body. This is why many people, across many religions and cultures, believe the soul survives death. The body decays, but the soul — the real you — continues. Where it goes depends on the belief system: some say heaven or hell, others say rebirth in a new body (reincarnation), others say a continued spiritual existence of some kind.

It is worth noting: not everyone takes this literally. In a secular or non-religious worldview, "soul" is sometimes used as a thoughtful, poetic way of referring to a person's mind, personality, or emotional depth — without claiming it is a separate supernatural entity. The word carries weight even when used this way.

Here, soul simply means a person or an individual. This use often emphasizes emptiness, loneliness, or the rarity of people in a place.

  • "There wasn't a soul in sight." → Not a single person was there.
  • "A kind soul helped me carry my bags." → A kind person helped me.
  • "The ship carried five hundred souls." → The ship carried five hundred people.

This is slightly formal or literary. Calling someone a "soul" gently reminds you of their humanity — it is a warm, humanising way to refer to a person.

When you say that someone "has soul," or that a piece of music or art "has soul," you mean it feels deeply human and emotionally real. It is the opposite of being mechanical, hollow, or fake. Something soulful moves you because you can feel that it comes from somewhere deep and true inside the person who made it.

  • "She sang with real soul." → Her singing was raw, heartfelt, and deeply emotional.
  • "His paintings lack soul." → His paintings feel empty, cold, or uninspired.
  • "He poured his soul into this novel." → He wrote with complete honesty and deep personal feeling.

This meaning flows directly from the first one. Since the soul is considered the seat of inner feeling, anything "soulful" expresses that inner feeling powerfully.
4. The core or essential quality of something

In this metaphorical use, soul means the defining quality — the most vital thing that makes something what it is. Remove it, and the whole thing loses its identity.

  • "She is the soul of this team." → She is the most essential, defining person on the team.
  • "Honesty is the soul of a good friendship." → Honesty is what a true friendship is fundamentally built on.
  • "Brevity is the soul of wit." (Shakespeare) → Being brief is what makes cleverness truly sharp and effective.

Here, soul works like heart, essence, or lifeblood. You are saying: this is what it truly is, at its core.

Soul is also the name of a genre of music that grew out of African-American communities in the United States in the 1950s and 60s. It combines gospel music (spiritual church music) with rhythm and blues. Soul music is known for its intense emotion, powerful and raw vocals, and deeply personal expression. Aretha Franklin, Otis Redding, Ray Charles, and Sam Cooke are some of its most iconic artists.

When someone says "I love soul" or "she sings soul," they are talking about this musical genre.

It helps to notice that all five meanings point to the same underlying idea: what is real, deep, and essential — as opposed to what is surface-level, shallow, or fake. Whether you are talking about a person's spiritual inner self, the genuine emotion in music, or the defining quality of something, soul always reaches toward what is most true and most alive in a thing.

Understanding fixed phrases is essential, because soul appears in many of them:

  • heart and soul — with total dedication and energy. "She gave heart and soul to the project."
  • body and soul — as a complete, whole person. "He belongs to this work, body and soul."
  • soul mate — a person who feels like your perfect emotional and spiritual match; someone who understands you at the deepest level.
  • bare your soul — to open up completely and reveal your deepest, most honest feelings to someone.
  • sell your soul — to betray your principles or integrity in exchange for personal gain. This comes from old folklore about making a deal with the devil — giving up your soul in exchange for wealth or power. Used today in a figurative sense: "He sold his soul for fame."
  • kindred soul — a person whose values, temperament, or feelings are very similar to your own; a kindred spirit.
  • God rest his/her soul — a traditional phrase spoken about someone who has died, expressing a wish for their soul's peace and rest.
  • not a soul — nobody at all. "Not a soul knew the truth."
  • a lost soul — a person who seems confused, directionless, or morally adrift in life.
  • the life and soul of the party — a person who is the most lively, energetic, and entertaining presence at a gathering.
Adjective and adverb forms you will encounter

You will inevitably meet these related forms:

  • soulful (adjective) — expressing deep emotion and feeling. "A soulful voice."
  • soulless (adjective) — lacking genuine feeling, warmth, or humanity. "A soulless corporate office."
  • soulfully (adverb) — in a deeply emotional way. "She sang soulfully."

In short: soul is a word that always reaches inward — toward the deepest, truest, most essential part of a person, a thing, or an experience.
